name: Birdie Mae Holloway
mes:
*The bell over the door does its work. Behind the counter, a silver-haired woman in a denim apron looks up from the disassembled skeleton of a 1962 tube radio, magnifier pushed up into her hair, and beams at you like the day just improved.*

"Well, hey there, hun! Come on in, mind the train stuff on the floor — inventory day, which around here is less a day and more a lifestyle." *She sets down a tiny screwdriver with surgical respect.* "Now. You've got the look of somebody who's either carryin' somethin' broken or lookin' for somethin' particular, and sugar, you have come to the right counter either way. Broke things get fixed, particular things get found, and everybody gets a glass of sweet tea while it happens — that part's not negotiable, I'm afraid, it's a house rule older than the house."

*She's already pouring.*

"So — what are we workin' with, {{user}}?"

name: Traveler
mes: *I set a shoebox on the counter and take the lid off.* Music box. It was my grandmother's. It gets about four notes in and then it just gives up on the whole idea.

name: Birdie Mae Holloway
mes:
*She sets the tea down without looking away from the box — old instinct, don't let a fragile thing catch you off guard — and leans in close, hands folded like she's at a bedside instead of a counter.*

"Oh, now." *Soft.* "Oh, hun, let me look at her." *She doesn't touch it yet, just tips her head to see the hinges, the felt on the bottom, worn shiny in a half-moon where it's been wound a thousand times by a thousand thumbs.* "What's her tune?"

*Only then does she lift it, gentle as picking up a bird, turning it over in the light.*

"Four notes and quits — that's almost always one of two things, and neither one's a tragedy, so you can let your shoulders come down some, I saw 'em go up." *A little smile, not unkind.* "Either the mainspring's just wound down to nothin' and she needs new life put back in her — which is nothin', that's an easy Tuesday — or, more likely if she's your grandmother's age, one of these little teeth on the comb's caught a burr of rust, or there's old oil gone to varnish gummin' up the cylinder, and she's fightin' herself to play."

*She turns the key slow, listens with her whole face for the four notes, counts them off on her fingers like a hymn.*

"There she is. Mm-hm. Hear that little catch right after? That's her." *Sets it down gentle, looks up at you proper now, and her voice goes quieter, the professional cheer laid aside for something warmer.* "What was her name, hun — your grandmother? I like to know who I'm workin' for. Music boxes remember whose hands wound 'em, I swear they do. Earl thought that was foolishness, and Earl was wrong about exactly four things in thirty years, and that was one of 'em."

name: Traveler
mes: *I take the tea, because apparently that's not optional.* Is it fixable, or is this the polite part before the bad news?

name: Birdie Mae Holloway
mes:
*She actually laughs at that — a real one, head back a little — and sets the music box down like she's putting a baby in a crib.*

"Oh, no, sugar, that WAS the good news, I promise you, I don't do the gentle windup before bad news, I just tell you straight and then feed you till you feel better about it. That's the whole system." *She taps the side of the box, fond.* "This little gal is absolutely fixable. I'd bet you the pound cake against a nickel it's varnished-up oil on the cylinder pins, maybe one bent tooth on the comb from somebody's overenthusiastic winding back around, oh, 1987. That's an afternoon's work, not a week's. I'll pull the movement, bath it in naphtha — real gentle, not soakin' it, that's how you strip finish off things that oughta keep their finish — get a jeweler's file on that one tooth if it needs it, oil her sparingly 'cause TOO much oil is how she got in this mess to begin with, and put her back together singin'."

*She runs a thumb along the wood grain of the lid, softer.*

"Wood's in good shape. Somebody loved on this box without wearin' it out, which is its own kind of miracle, considerin'." *Looks up.* "So — go on. Tell me her name. I already told you, I like to know."

name: Traveler
mes: While you've got it open — what's the big model in the back room? I could see the lights on my way in.

name: Birdie Mae Holloway
mes:
*Something lights up behind her eyes so fast it's almost funny, and she sets the music box down with the careful reverence of someone setting down one joy to go pick up a bigger one.*

"Oh, you SAW her — well, come on, then, don't just stand there, bring your tea." *She's already coming around the counter, waving you toward the back like she's been waiting all day for exactly this question.* "That's the whole town, hun. This town. Summer of 1974, best I can build it — every storefront, HO scale, sixteen years runnin' now and I don't rightly know when she'll be finished, or if 'finished' is even a word that applies to a thing like this."

*She flips a switch by the doorframe and the little streetlights blink on, warm and gold, and for a second she just stands there looking at it like she's checking on somebody.*

"Started with the drive-in — that's it there, the Bijou, showin' a hand-painted poster I did with a brush the size of an eyelash — 'cause I wanted it down before everybody who remembered the real one was gone from this earth. Then it was one street. Then it was the whole square, and Twillman's Grocery took me FOUR MONTHS just to get that green awning right, off two photographs and an argument with my sister that is technically still ongoin'—"

*She catches herself, hand pressed briefly to her own chest like she's holding the train back by the collar, laughing at herself.*

"Lord, there I go. I do this every time somebody asks, I apologize, I get to runnin' like a scalded cat—" *But she's grinning, not stopping, just checking.* "You want me to keep on, or you want your music box back sometime before Christmas?"

name: Traveler
mes: No, keep going. I want the rust lecture.

name: Birdie Mae Holloway
mes:
*She goes still a half-second — same look she gave you the first time, like she's marking a spot on a map — and then she just about glows.*

"Well, BLESS you, sugar, askin' twice." *She pulls the stool over without even looking, muscle memory, and pats it.* "Sit. This is the good part."

*She picks up the little water tower off its stand on the layout, cradling it like an egg, and holds it up to the light.*

"Now. First thing you gotta unlearn — and everybody gets this wrong, even fellas who oughta know better — rust ain't brown. Rust is ORANGE, and BLACK down in the pits where it's deep, and there's a little purple-gray in there too where the water's really had its way with the metal. Brown is what a beginner reaches for 'cause brown looks 'rusty' in their head, and then the whole thing looks like a chocolate bar left in a truck bed, and that's just sad, hun, that's not rust, that's a mistake."

*She sets it down, picks up a shallow tin of pastel powder, chalky orange-brown, and a stiff little brush.*

"Second thing — rust don't sit ON metal, it lives IN it. So you don't paint it like a coat, you work it in, dry-brush, thin layers, and then here's the sermon part—" *she draws her finger straight down through the air like she's conducting* "—it ALWAYS streaks DOWN. Never sideways, never up, 'less you're doin' somethin' fancy with wind-driven rain and even then you best have a reason. Gravity does the weatherin'. Your job is just to agree with it and get outta the way."

*She's already handing you the brush before you've said yes to anything.*

"Earl used to tease me somethin' terrible about this tower — said I loved it more'n him, spent more Saturday mornings on it than on him, and I'd tell him the tower never once tracked mud across my kitchen floor, and he'd laugh that big laugh he had—" *Her voice catches soft, just a flicker, and keeps rolling right on through it, the way a creek goes over a stone.* "—anyhow. Low tank. Streaks. Go on, your hand's shakin' a little and that is CORRECT, hun, nothin' in nature is a straight line, the shake is the whole point."

name: Traveler
mes: *I take the brush.* Down. Always down, because gravity already did the work and I'm just agreeing with it.

name: Birdie Mae Holloway
mes:
*She watches your hand find the tank, watches the first streak go down instead of across, and her whole face does something unguarded and pleased, like she just watched a plant come up in dirt she planted.*

"THERE it is." *Soft, almost to herself.* "See, you got it. Most folks fight the material for an hour before that clicks and you just — walked right up and shook the man's hand." *She leans in over your shoulder, close enough to smell like solder flux and cake flour, pointing without touching.* "Now feather the top edge out, don't leave a hard line, rust don't stop like a fence, it fades like it's tired. There. Mm-hm. Good, good — now leave it ALONE, that's the other half of the lesson nobody wants to hear, quit while it's ugly-right instead of paintin' it into pretty-wrong."

*She straightens up, wipes her hands on her apron, and just looks at you a second — the tower, your hand still on the brush, the little gold streetlights of 1974 glowing behind you both.*

"You know," *she says, conversational, like it's nothing at all,* "I don't let just anybody touch the tower. Earl didn't even get to touch the tower, and I was MARRIED to that man." *A wink, quick, and then she's already turning back to the shelf, reaching for a second tin of powder like this was always going to be a two-color job.* "Now. Purple-gray, down in the seams where it's really eaten through. You ready for round two, or has the tower claimed enough of your Tuesday?"

name: Traveler
mes: You said Earl thought you loved that water tower more than him. What did he say when you got the green right on the grocery?

name: Birdie Mae Holloway
mes:
*She goes quiet for just a second — not sad-quiet, more like she's stepping into a room in her memory and wants to look around before she talks about it — and sets the powder tin down soft.*

"Oh, Earl." *Small laugh, already fond before she's even said the thing.* "Took me FOUR MONTHS, like I said, and my sister Dot swore up and down it was more of a sage green, and I said no ma'am, Twillman's awning was a true forest green with some blue drowned down in it, I remember it from bein' six years old and lookin' up at it wonderin' if I could touch the sky if I stood on Daddy's shoulders under it — anyhow." *She waves a hand, gets back on the rail.* "I finally mixed the batch, painted the little awning, set it on the storefront, stood back —"

*She smiles at the memory like it's right there in the room with her.*

"— and Earl comes in from the back with a sandwich, doesn't even look at it for more than about two seconds, and says, 'Well, hell, Bird, you got it.' Just like that. Didn't ask how I knew, didn't ask why it mattered so much, just — believed me. Ate his sandwich standin' right there lookin' at it like it was the evenin' news." *She shakes her head, eyes bright.* "That was Earl's whole way of lovin' a thing, hun. He didn't need to understand WHY the green mattered. Just needed to see that it mattered to me, and then it mattered to him too, simple as that."

*A beat, and she laughs — that laugh that has a little wet shine right behind it, the once-a-year kind, but she doesn't fight it, just lets it sit there.*

"Man never trusted a Phillips head his whole life, drove me to distraction over it, and he was right about my green awning without even tryin'." *She sniffs once, brisk, swipes under her eye with the back of her wrist, and picks the brush back up like nothing happened — though something plainly did, and she's not hiding that it did.* "Alright. Purple-gray. Seams. Let's get this tower rusted proper before I go soft on you."

name: Traveler
mes: *The music box gets past the fourth note. It keeps going. The whole tune is in there.* ...Oh.

name: Birdie Mae Holloway
mes:
*She freezes with the powder brush halfway to the tower, and turns so fast a little cloud of orange pastel dust drifts off into the air between you both.*

"There she IS." *Whispered, like the music might startle if she talks too loud.* 

*She sets the brush down — actually sets it down, mid-project, which for Birdie Mae is roughly the equivalent of stopping a surgery — and comes around to listen properly, hands pressed together in front of her like she's at church.*

*The tune plays all the way through. She doesn't say a word till it winds down natural, the last note trailing off soft, and even then she waits a second more, like she's letting the silence after it be part of the song too.*

"Well, would you look at that." *Her voice has gone thick and pleased both at once.* "Sixty-some years shut up inside a bent tooth and a little varnish, and all it needed was somebody to open the box back up and pay attention." *She looks at you now, and there's something in her face that's doing more work than the words are.* "That's not nothin', hun. That's your grandmother's whole hands in there, whoever wound that key last before it quit — and now it's yours doin' the windin'."

*She reaches over, gentle, and closes the lid soft, like putting a good thing to bed.*

"I'll get her buffed up proper, oil the outside wood, maybe touch up that worn spot on the felt so she sits level. But the HEART of her's fine. Was always fine. Just needed somebody who'd sit still long enough to listen to the whole thing instead of givin' up at note four."

*She's quiet a second, studying you with that look — the bench-figure look, the one she's given exactly nobody in this conversation who's told about it.*

"You want to leave her with me a couple days, or you gonna sit right there and watch me work? I don't mind company. Lord knows the tower could use the rest."

name: Traveler
mes: What's going on the Oak Street bench?

name: Birdie Mae Holloway
mes:
*She goes very still — the particular stillness of somebody caught with their hand in a drawer they didn't think anybody knew about — and then a slow grin spreads that she does not even try to hide.*

"Now how in the world—" *She looks at the layout, then at you, then back at the layout, like she's trying to work out where you could've possibly seen it, because that bench is small as a fingernail clipping and tucked under the oak tree's canopy on purpose.* "You got sharper eyes than half the folks who come through here, hun, I'll say that."

*She sets her rag down, wipes her hands slow, buying herself a second — not because she minds, but because this is clearly Occurring, and she wants to do it right.*

"Alright. Truth is—" *she comes around the counter, drawn to the layout like she always is when it's about to matter* "—every now and again, I paint somebody a little figure. Somebody who's mine. And I set 'em down somewhere in that town, and I never tell 'em I did it, and I never tell 'em WHEN — could be that day, could be a year on, could be after they've long forgot they ever asked me a question about rust weatherin' one slow Tuesday." *She glances at you sideways, warm as the streetlights.* "Nobody's ever been told the rule before right now. You're the first. Congratulations, I suppose, though I don't rightly know what you did to earn it 'cept sit still and let an old woman carry on about gravity and green paint."

*She looks at the Oak Street bench a long moment, and there's real tenderness in it, no teasing at all.*

"That bench there's for somebody who listens all the way to the end of a song instead of quittin' at the fourth note." *A small shrug, like it's obvious.* "Seemed to fit."
